body: Bruyere Research Institute / deprescribing.org (Pottie et al.)
guidelineTitle: Deprescribing benzodiazepine receptor agonists: Evidence-based clinical practice guideline
recommendation: "We recommend that deprescribing (tapering slowly) of BZRAs be offered to elderly adults (>= 65 years) who take BZRAs, regardless of duration of use, and suggest that deprescribing (tapering slowly) be offered to adults aged 18 to 64 who have used BZRAs for more than 4 weeks."
strength: Strong for >=65 y; weak ('suggest') for 18-64 y (GRADE)

citation.authors: Pottie K, Thompson W, Davies S, et al.
citation.title: Deprescribing benzodiazepine receptor agonists: Evidence-based clinical practice guideline

conflictsOfInterest: Abstract: 'members disclosed conflicts of interest'; details not read
notes: Applies to primary insomnia or comorbid insomnia with comorbidities managed; not to other sleep disorders or untreated anxiety/depression. BZRA = benzodiazepines plus Z-drugs.

body: Choosing Wisely Canada / Canadian Geriatrics Society
guidelineTitle: Geriatrics: Recommendation 2
recommendation: "Don't use benzodiazepines or other sedative-hypnotics in older adults as first choice for insomnia, agitation or delirium." Supporting text: number needed to treat for better sleep is 13, number needed to harm is 6; CBT and taper protocols help discontinuation.

citation.authors: Canadian Geriatrics Society
citation.title: Choosing Wisely Canada: Geriatrics recommendations

notes: Similar recommendations from other Canadian societies (psychiatry, hospital pharmacists) per search snippets, not read directly.

country: Canada (Ontario, Centre for Effective Practice tool; also linked by Alberta)
body: Centre for Effective Practice (CEP)
guidelineTitle: Management of Chronic Insomnia
recommendation: "CBT-I is recommended as the initial treatment for chronic insomnia." "Pharmacotherapy should be considered as adjunctive therapy to CBT-I." Start lowest dose, short duration (e.g. 1-2 weeks); "pharmacotherapy should be used no longer than ~1 month". In older adults, "the safest and best studied sleep medication ... is doxepin (<= 6mg/day)"; avoid benzodiazepines in the elderly.

citation.authors: Centre for Effective Practice; Ontario College of Family Physicians; Nurse Practitioners' Association of Ontario
citation.title: Management of Chronic Insomnia (tool)

conflictsOfInterest: Funded by Ontario Ministry of Health (Knowledge Translation in Primary Care Initiative); panel COI not stated on page
notes: Alberta's former TOP 'Assessment to Management of Adult Insomnia' guideline (Dec 2015) is no longer hosted as a document: the Alberta Medical Association page now links only to the TOP sleep questionnaire and this CEP tool, and says ACTT 'no longer develops or updates' single-topic CPGs.

country: Canada (Ontario, Centre for Effective Practice tool)
body: Centre for Effective Practice (CEP)
guidelineTitle: Management of Chronic Insomnia
recommendation: Ontario Drug Benefit coverage shown in tool: doxepin, trazodone, temazepam covered; zopiclone not covered; zolpidem, melatonin, valerian uncertain. Online CBT-I listed as paid (e.g. Sleepio US$300/12 months).

citation.authors: Centre for Effective Practice; Ontario College of Family Physicians; Nurse Practitioners' Association of Ontario
citation.title: Management of Chronic Insomnia (tool)

notes: 2017 coverage snapshot; verify against current Ontario formulary. Notable that zopiclone (Canada's most-used Z-drug) was listed as not ODB-covered.

body: Centre for Effective Practice (CEP)
guidelineTitle: Management of Chronic Insomnia
recommendation: Taper BZRAs by "no more than diazepam 5mg or clonazepam 0.25mg equivalent per week" (slower below 20 mg diazepam-equivalent), or reduce 10% every 1-2 weeks until 20% remains, then 5% every 2-4 weeks; follow up every 1-4 weeks; consider CBT.

citation.authors: Centre for Effective Practice; Ontario College of Family Physicians; Nurse Practitioners' Association of Ontario
citation.title: Management of Chronic Insomnia (tool)

body: Ontario Ministry of Health (no official source found)
guidelineTitle: CBT-I public coverage
recommendation: No official source found showing CBT-I is publicly covered in Ontario: psychologist services are outside OHIP; Ontario Structured Psychotherapy officially covers depression and anxiety. Only retailer blogs claim insomnia is accepted.
notes: Absence is the finding: unlike Australia (Better Access) Canada has no national subsidised CBT-I route found. Kalman: worth a manual check of OSP intake criteria.

body: Canada's Drug Agency (CDA-AMC, formerly CADTH)
guidelineTitle: Daridorexant (Quviviq) reimbursement recommendation (SR0862)
recommendation: "CDEC recommends that daridorexant not be reimbursed for the management of adult patients with insomnia" characterized by difficulties with sleep onset and/or sleep maintenance. Initial meeting 28 May 2025; reconsideration 24 Sept 2025 upheld it. Reasons: unclear whether benefit is clinically meaningful; no comparison with other insomnia drugs.

citation.authors: Canada's Drug Agency (CDA-AMC), Canadian Drug Expert Committee
citation.title: Daridorexant (Quviviq) reimbursement recommendation (SR0862)

notes: Sponsor asked for listing in moderate-severe chronic insomnia when CBT-I is inappropriate, unavailable or failed (ISI >= 15). Health Canada NOC for Quviviq: 28 April 2023 (from CDA clinical review).

body: Health Canada
guidelineTitle: Notice of Compliance: Quviviq (daridorexant)
recommendation: Approved for "the management of adult patients with insomnia, characterized by difficulties with sleep onset and/or sleep maintenance." NOC date 28 April 2023.

citation.authors: CDA-AMC
citation.title: Daridorexant (Quviviq) Clinical Review SR0862r

body: Canada's Drug Agency (CDA-AMC, formerly CADTH)
guidelineTitle: Lemborexant (Dayvigo) reimbursement recommendation (SR0895, resubmission)
recommendation: CDEC "recommends that lemborexant not be reimbursed for the treatment of insomnia." Second 'do not reimburse' (first 10 Jan 2023; resubmission for chronic insomnia disorder, reconsideration 17 Dec 2025). New fall-risk observational studies could not show lower fall risk than other drugs.

citation.authors: Canada's Drug Agency (CDA-AMC), Canadian Drug Expert Committee
citation.title: Lemborexant (Dayvigo) reimbursement recommendation (SR0895, resubmission)

notes: Health Canada NOC 4 Nov 2020 (Summary Basis of Decision, via search snippet; not opened). BC PharmaCare non-benefit decision 14 Mar 2024 (search snippet). So in Canada both licensed DORAs are approved but not publicly funded; suvorexant is not marketed in Canada (not checked directly).

body: Health Canada (Natural and Non-prescription Health Products Directorate)
guidelineTitle: Melatonin - Oral monograph (NHP)
recommendation: Melatonin is sold as a licensed Natural Health Product (non-prescription). All licensed melatonin NHPs are for adults only; none authorised for children. Monograph doses commonly cited 0.1-10 mg/day; label advice not to use more than 4 weeks without consulting a health professional. Health Canada consulted on making paediatric sleep use prescription-only.

citation.authors: Health Canada
citation.title: Monograph: Melatonin - Oral

notes: Details from search summaries of Health Canada pages; monograph itself not opened. Contrast: Australia/NZ prescription or pharmacist-only; Brazil food supplement capped at 0.21 mg.

body: Canadian Thoracic Society (CTS)
guidelineTitle: Canadian Thoracic Society 2011 guideline update: diagnosis and treatment of sleep disordered breathing
recommendation: "Patients with suspected severe OSAS, and patients working in safety-critical occupations should be investigated within four weeks of the referral to a diagnostic sleep facility." Same for unstable heart disease, recent stroke, heart failure, refractory hypertension, pregnancy etc. "All patients within six months of the referral".

citation.authors: Fleetham J, Ayas N, Bradley D, et al.; CTS Sleep Disordered Breathing Committee
citation.title: Canadian Thoracic Society 2011 guideline update: diagnosis and treatment of sleep disordered breathing

conflictsOfInterest: Committee members declared potential conflicts at appointment, updated per CTS COI policy; CTS states editorial independence
notes: No newer adult CTS OSA guideline found (2026 CTS/CSS guideline is paediatric only, PMID 41887281). One of few guidelines anywhere to set explicit wait-time targets.

body: Canadian Thoracic Society (CTS)
guidelineTitle: Canadian Thoracic Society 2011 guideline update: diagnosis and treatment of sleep disordered breathing
recommendation: Level I attended PSG "remains the accepted standard ... and is the test of choice when readily available." Level III portable studies "can be used to confirm the diagnosis of OSAS and institute appropriate treatment in patients with a moderate to high pretest probability" when part of a package of care with physician expertise and PSG back-up.

body: Canadian Thoracic Society (CTS)
guidelineTitle: Canadian Thoracic Society 2011 guideline update: diagnosis and treatment of sleep disordered breathing
recommendation: "Conventional CPAP at a fixed pressure is the primary treatment for patients with OSAS." "APAP is an alternative effective treatment to fixed CPAP for OSAS in the absence of comorbid diseases and conditions." Treat asymptomatic patients with significant cardiovascular disease "especially if the AHI is 19/h or greater" (2C).

body: Ontario Ministry of Health, Assistive Devices Program (ADP)
guidelineTitle: Respiratory Equipment and Supplies: applicant information (4793-67E, 2025/01)
recommendation: "ADP pays 75% of the ADP approved price" for CPAP/APAP/BPAP; may pay 100% for people on Ontario Works, ODSP or ACSD. "To receive funding assistance for CPAP/APAP/BPAP systems you must be assessed by a physician who works at a sleep clinic registered with the ADP." Form signed by patient, prescribing physician or NP, and ADP-registered vendor; review about six weeks.

body: Australasian Sleep Association + Sleep Health Foundation + RACGP + Australian Psychological Society + Pharmaceutical Society of Australia + APNA (joint position statement)
guidelineTitle: Management of adult insomnia in Australia (joint position statement)
recommendation: "Multi-component Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for insomnia (CBTi) is the recommended 'first-line' treatment for insomnia", effective across settings, comorbidities and modes (individual, group, telehealth, self-guided digital). Sleep hygiene advice "not an adequate stand-alone treatment for chronic insomnia". "Clinicians should discuss CBTi options with all patients with insomnia as the first-line management approach."

recommendation: Insomnia is an eligible condition under Medicare's Better Access initiative: GP prepares a Mental Health Treatment Plan; rebate for "up to 10 in-person or tele-health consultations each calendar year" (gaps can exceed rebate). body: Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) / Poisons Standard
guidelineTitle: Notice of final decision to amend the Poisons Standard in relation to melatonin
status: current (change proposed for March 2026 ACMS meeting; outcome not confirmed)
recommendation: Schedule 3 (pharmacist-only) for modified-release tablets <= 2 mg melatonin for short-term monotherapy of primary insomnia with poor sleep quality in adults aged 55 or over, packs <= 30 tablets; all other melatonin Schedule 4 (prescription). A 2023 decision added Schedule 3 immediate-release <= 5 mg for jet lag in adults (no product marketed at time of report).

recommendation: Suvorexant (Belsomra, MSD) approved as a new chemical entity at 15 and 20 mg (AusPAR March 2015, updated June 2018). Lemborexant (Dayvigo) is also on the Australian market (Schedule 4, in AMH for chronic insomnia). Neither PBS-listed.

body: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners (RACGP)
guidelineTitle: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice, Part B: Benzodiazepines
status: stale (published 2015; page notes may not reflect current evidence)
recommendation: "First-line therapy should be non-drug interventions" and CBT "should therefore be offered to patients, including older adults" (Level A). "Short-term or intermittent dosing of benzodiazepines should be used to reduce the risk of tolerance and dependence" (Level B). "Long-term use, beyond 4 weeks, should be uncommon". Stepped approach to discontinuation.
strength: Level A (non-drug first line); Level B (short/intermittent)

body: Australian Government, Medicare Benefits Schedule (MBS)
guidelineTitle: MBS items 12203 (attended PSG) and 12250 (unattended home study)
recommendation: Item 12250 (home study, adults 18+) is payable if either (i) a medical practitioner (e.g. GP) refers to a sleep or respiratory physician who determines high probability of symptomatic moderate-severe OSA "based on a STOP-Bang score of 3 or more, an OSA50 score of 5 or more or a high risk score on the Berlin Questionnaire, and an Epworth Sleepiness Scale score of 8 or more"; or (ii) the specialist sees the patient (face-to-face or video) and decides a test is needed. Item 12203 (lab PSG) has the same gate plus listed indications (e.g. not suitable for home study, central apnoea, hypoventilation).

citation.authors: Australian Government Department of Health
citation.title: MBS Online item 12250

notes: The questionnaire route lets a GP get a home test without the patient seeing the specialist first, but a sleep/respiratory physician still has to sign off the referral; it is not GP-ordered testing outright. Some secondary sources still quote STOP-Bang >= 4 (pre-March 2021).

body: Australian Government, Medicare Benefits Schedule (MBS)
guidelineTitle: MBS item 12204 (CPAP titration study)
recommendation: Attended PAP titration study payable when need is decided by a qualified adult sleep medicine practitioner or respiratory physician, who has seen the patient (face-to-face or video) and established the breathing disorder causes the symptoms; patient has not had PAP in the previous 6 months. Medicare does not subsidise the CPAP device itself.

citation.authors: Australian Government Department of Health
citation.title: MBS Online item 12204

notes: 'No Medicare subsidy for the device' comes from secondary (retailer) sources plus absence of any MBS/PBS item; device funding is state-run (see Queensland row) or private/health-fund extras.

body: Queensland Health
guidelineTitle: Queensland Health Sleep Disorders Program (QHSDP)
recommendation: Free CPAP loan for Queensland residents holding a Pensioner Concession Card, Health Care Card or DVA white card, with "significant sleep apnoea" diagnosed at a QHSDP Prescriber Centre, managed by an RACP-accredited sleep physician; must first rent a device for a "minimum 2-month home treatment trial with average usage of at least 4 hours per night"; buy own mask. Access needs GP or specialist referral.

citation.authors: Queensland Government
citation.title: Queensland Health Sleep Disorders Program

notes: Means-tested and state-specific. NSW equivalent (EnableNSW) needs pension concession card, severity criteria and proof of use; co-payment $100/year for pensioners (from search summary of NSW Health pages, not opened). Clinician-facing QLD page bot-blocked.

body: bpacnz (Best Practice Advocacy Centre)
guidelineTitle: Managing insomnia: Part 2 - pharmacological treatment
recommendation: "Non-pharmacological interventions are the preferred treatment for insomnia." Hypnotics "should be used for a maximum of four weeks (but often less)"; short-acting hypnotics "should be prescribed for no more than two to three weeks", ideally a few nights. Temazepam, triazolam and zopiclone are the medicines indicated for insomnia. No OTC products incl. sedating antihistamines recommended; limited evidence for quetiapine.

citation.authors: bpacnz
citation.title: Managing insomnia: Part 2 - pharmacological treatment

notes: 2021 bpac article: zopiclone is NZ's most dispensed funded hypnotic. No DORA mentioned; none appears to be approved/funded in NZ (not checked against Medsafe directly).

body: Medsafe / PHARMAC (via Medsafe MARC paper, March 2026)
guidelineTitle: Melatonin safety profile in adults (MARC meeting 12 March 2026)
recommendation: Since 10 Oct 2025, adults 18+ can buy from pharmacies (pharmacy-only) up to 30 days of melatonin for primary insomnia (immediate-release <= 3 mg or modified-release <= 2 mg) or 10 days for jet lag (IR <= 5 mg). Adults 55+ can still get up to 13 weeks after pharmacist consultation. Otherwise prescription. PHARMAC funds modified-release 2 mg (Vigisom brand) only for patients <= 18 years meeting Special Authority criteria; unsubsidised for adult insomnia.

citation.authors: Medsafe Medicines Adverse Reactions Committee
citation.title: Melatonin safety profile in adults

notes: NZ is now more permissive than Australia (where adults under 55 need a prescription). bpac 2017 also said melatonin is unsubsidised for adult insomnia.

body: Associação Brasileira do Sono (ABS) + Associação Brasileira de Medicina do Sono (ABMS)
guidelineTitle: 2023 Guidelines on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Insomnia in Adults
recommendation: "Multicomponent CBT-I is recommended as the gold standard for treating chronic insomnia" (100% agreement). In-person and group CBT-I: Recommended, evidence Level 1; online CBT-I Level 2 and "not inferior to in-person"; digital Level 1 (78.1% agreement). "Sleep hygiene is not recommended as an isolated form of intervention."
strength: Delphi consensus (>=75% agreement) + Oxford CEBM evidence level 1

body: Associação Brasileira do Sono (ABS) + Associação Brasileira de Medicina do Sono (ABMS)
guidelineTitle: 2023 Guidelines on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Insomnia in Adults
recommendation: Melatonin NOT Recommended for adult insomnia (Level 2; 76% onset, 88% maintenance), but special statement: "Melatonin can be used to treat initial insomnia in the elderly and children with autism spectrum disorder." Also NOT Recommended: quetiapine (Level 5), gabapentin (Level 5), valerian (Level 2), cannabinoids (Level 3), promethazine, hydroxyzine, dimenhydrinate (Level 5).

body: ANVISA (Agência Nacional de Vigilância Sanitária)
guidelineTitle: Zolpidem prescription rules (RDC 871 and 877/2024; Comunicado GGMON 002/2024)
recommendation: From 1 Aug 2024 all zolpidem products, at any dose, need the blue 'Notificação de Receita B' (controlled prescription; prescriber registered with local health surveillance). The old exemption treating doses up to 10 mg like List C1 (ordinary two-copy prescription) was removed. Original reasoning (press summary): "não há dados científicos que demonstrem que concentrações de até 10 mg mereçam um critério regulatório diferenciado" (no scientific data show doses up to 10 mg deserve different rules). Packs move to black stripe (tarja preta) by 1 Dec 2024.

citation.authors: ANVISA
citation.title: Comunicado GGMON 002/2024: Medicamento zolpidem terá alteração no tipo de receita para prescrição e venda

notes: ANVISA page shows only title; details from Brazilian press and CFM. Driven by rising zolpidem misuse; see also Brazilian Academy of Neurology 2025 Z-drug dependence guideline (Stelzer et al., PMID 41187937, DOI 10.1055/s-0045-1812323), which restates the no-more-than-4-weeks rule.

body: ANVISA
guidelineTitle: Instrução Normativa 28/2018 amendment: melatonin in food supplements
recommendation: Since Oct 2021 (Dicol decision 14 Oct 2021) melatonin is allowed in food supplements without prescription for adults (reported as over 19), max 0.21 mg/day; label warning against use by pregnant or breastfeeding women, children, and people doing tasks needing constant attention. Original: "Não foram aprovadas alegações" de benefício (no health claims approved, i.e. cannot be sold 'for sleep').

citation.authors: ANVISA
citation.title: Voto 80/2021 DIRE3 (melatonina em suplementos alimentares)

notes: 0.21 mg is a tenth or less of the 2 mg dose used in Australia/NZ/Europe. Before 2021, melatonin only via prescription at compounding pharmacies.

body: Sociedade Brasileira de Pneumologia e Tisiologia (SBPT)
guidelineTitle: Brazilian Thoracic Association Consensus on Sleep-disordered Breathing
recommendation: High-risk patients (by screening) "can be tested either at home or in the sleep laboratory"; low-risk should be tested in the lab. A negative or technically poor home study with high suspicion should be followed by in-lab PSG. Screening tools can route high-risk patients to home testing "thus trimming the waiting lists at sleep laboratories."

citation.authors: Duarte RLM, Togeiro SMGP, Palombini LO, et al.
citation.title: Brazilian Thoracic Association Consensus on Sleep-disordered Breathing

notes: Brazilian Sleep Association OSA-specific guideline not found beyond this SBPT consensus and allied-health guidelines (physiotherapy 2022, speech therapy 2023).

body: Sociedade Brasileira de Pneumologia e Tisiologia (SBPT)
guidelineTitle: Brazilian Thoracic Association Consensus on Sleep-disordered Breathing
recommendation: "Positive pressure therapy is the treatment of choice for individuals with moderate-to-severe OSA." Adherence defined as CPAP >= 4 h/night on >= 70% of nights in the first 3 months. Other options: positional therapy, alcohol avoidance, exercise, weight loss, oral appliances, surgery.

body: Sistema Único de Saúde (SUS) / NATJUS-RJ technical opinions
guidelineTitle: CPAP access in SUS
recommendation: No Ministry of Health clinical protocol (PCDT) for OSA; CPAP not assessed by CONITEC; not on any national, Rio state or municipal SUS dispensing list and no outpatient SIGTAP code. Original: "não há PCDT publicado pelo Ministério da Saúde para apneia do sono" (no Ministry of Health protocol published for sleep apnoea).

body: Asociación Argentina de Medicina Respiratoria (AAMR)
guidelineTitle: Guías prácticas de diagnóstico y tratamiento del síndrome de apneas e hipopneas obstructivas del sueño: Actualización 2018
recommendation: "La evidencia disponible muestra que la PR realizada en el domicilio del paciente es comparable a la PSG realizada en el laboratorio de sueño para el diagnóstico del SAHOS del adulto en pacientes con sospecha clínica. (Evidencia A)" (home respiratory polygraphy is comparable to lab PSG in adults with clinical suspicion). Expert reading needed with heart/lung disease, neuromuscular disease, stroke, chronic opioids. Valid study needs >= 4 h interpretable recording.

body: Asociación Argentina de Medicina Respiratoria (AAMR)
guidelineTitle: Guías prácticas de diagnóstico y tratamiento del síndrome de apneas e hipopneas obstructivas del sueño: Actualización 2018
recommendation: "La aplicación de presión positiva continua en la vía aérea (CPAP) durante el sueño es el tratamiento de elección para el SAHOS" (CPAP is the treatment of choice) (Recomendación A). Indicated for AHI >= 15/h, or AHI 5-14.9 with daytime sleepiness, cognitive deficit, or cardiovascular/metabolic/cerebrovascular disease (A). "La indicación, ajuste y control del tratamiento debe estar a cargo de un equipo profesional entrenado en Medicina del Sueño" (sleep-medicine team prescribes and follows). Auto-CPAP titration at home allowed (A).

citation.authors: Nogueira F, Borsini E, Cambursano H, et al. (AAMR)
citation.title: Guías prácticas de diagnóstico y tratamiento del síndrome de apneas e hipopneas obstructivas del sueño: Actualización 2018

notes: Oral appliances: custom, titratable devices recommended for those who suit them; surgery first-line only for fixable obstruction (e.g. tonsils).

body: Instituto Mexicano del Seguro Social (IMSS) / CENETEC clinical practice guideline
guidelineTitle: Guía de práctica clínica. Diagnóstico y tratamiento del insomnio en el adulto mayor
recommendation: For older adults: find and treat secondary causes, use non-drug therapy including sleep hygiene, then drugs. "No es recomendable comenzar el tratamiento con un hipnótico" before ruling out causative drugs/diseases. "Tampoco se recomienda el uso de neurolépticos, melatonina, antihistamínicos o benzodiacepinas de vida media larga" (antipsychotics, melatonin, antihistamines and long-acting benzodiazepines not recommended).
